            48                     ABRAMOVICH, OLSSON, AND VISTOLI

               With notation as in A.10, if U → X is a smooth surjection of schemes
            and MU denotes the pullback of MX , then it follows immediately from
            the definition that (X, MX ) → (S, MS ) is essentially semistable if and
            only if the morphism (U, MU ) → (S, MS ) is essentially semistable (the
            property of being semistable is local in the smooth topology on X). It
            follows that the notion of a morphism being essentially semistable extends
            to Artin stacks: If (X, MX) is an Artin stack with a fine log structure,
            and f : (X, MX) → (S, MS ) is a morphism to a fine log scheme, then f is
            essentially semistable if for some smooth surjection U → X with U a scheme
            the induced morphism of log schemes
 testmap    (A.10.2)                     (U, MX|U ) → (S, MS )
            is essentially semistable. As usual if for some smooth surjection U → X
            the morphism A.10.2 is essentially semistable then for any smooth surjec-
            tion V → X the induced morphism (V, MX|V ) → (S, MS ) is essentially
            semistable.
               As explained in [33, §3], if (X, MX ) → (S, MS ) is an essentially semistable
            morphism of log schemes, then for any geometric point s̄ → S there is a
            canonical induced map
                              sXs̄ : {singular points of Xs̄ } → Irr(MS,s̄ ),
            where Irr(MS,s̄ ) denotes the set of irreducible elements in the monoid MS,s̄ .
               If Y is an Artin stack over a field k, let π0 (Ysing ) denote the set of connected
            components of the complement of the maximal open substack U ⊂ Y which
            is smooth over k. Note that if Y′ → Y is a smooth morphism of k-stacks,
            then there is an induced map
                                          π0 (Y′sing ) → π0 (Ysing ).
            If Y′ → Y is also surjective then this map is also surjective.
            Definition A.11. Let f : (X, MX) → (S, MS ) be an essentially semistable
            morphism from a log Artin stack to a fine log scheme, and let s̄ → S be a

                       Appendix B. Remarks on Ext-groups and base change
                                       By Martin Olsson
    AppendixC
                    In this appendix we gather together some fairly standard results about
                 Ext-groups and base change, which will be used in the following appendix
                 C. We include the results here as there does not seem to be an adequate
                 treatment in the literature that covers the case when one does not have
                 boundedness of cohomology (such as for Artin stacks).

                 B.1. Base change for cohomology.
      B:setup    B.2. Let S be an integral noetherian scheme, and let f : X → S be a proper
                 algebraic stack over S. Let F be a coherent sheaf on X . For any morphism
                                                     g : S′ → S
                 we can then form the cartesian square
                                                           h
                                                     X′        // X

                                                    f′                f
                                                         g       
                                                     S′        // S,

                 and for every i ∈ Z we have a base change morphism
 B:basechange    (B.2.1)                       g∗ Ri f∗ F → Ri f∗′ h∗ F.
 T:basechange    Theorem B.3. With notation as in B.2, for every integer i ∈ Z there exists
                 a dense open subset U ⊂ S (which depends on i) such that for any morphism
                 g : S ′ → S which factors through U , the base change morphism (B.2.1) is
                 an isomorphism.
                             TWISTED YET TAME                                53

Proof. First of all, by shrinking on S we may assume that S is affine, say
S = Spec(R), and that F is flat over S. Furthermore, it suffices to show that
there exists a dense open subset U ⊂ Spec(R) such that for any morphism
of affine schemes
                         g : S ′ = Spec(R′ ) → Spec(R)
which factors through U , the natural map
                      H i (X , F) ⊗R R′ → H i (X ′ , h∗ F)
is an isomorphism.
   Let X· → X be a smooth hypercover of X , with each Xn a finite disjoint
union of affine schemes. For n ≥ 0 set
                             Fn := Γ(Xn , F|Xn ),
so we obtain a complex (using the standard Cech differentials)
                         C· : F 0 → F 1 → F 2 → · · ·
which computes the cohomology RΓ(X , F ).
  For any morphism of affine schemes
                        g : S ′ = Spec(R′ ) → Spec(R)
the base change of X· to S ′ is a smooth hypercover X·′ → X ′ which similarly
can be used to compute the cohomology of h∗ F. From this it follows that it
suffices to show that for any i ∈ Z there exists a dense open subset U ⊂ S
such that if g factors through U , then the natural map
                       H i (C · ) ⊗R R′ → H i (C · ⊗R R′ )
is an isomorphism (note that here C · ⊗R R′ is not the derived tensor product).
This follows from the following lemma.                                       ♠
Lemma B.4. Let R be a noetherian integral domain, and let C · be a complex
of flat R-modules such that for every j ∈ Z the R-module H j (C · ) is finitely
generated. Then for every i ∈ Z there exists an open subset U ⊂ Spec(R)
such that for every morphism Spec(R′ ) → U the natural map
                       H i (C · ) ⊗R R′ → H i (C · ⊗R R′ )
is an isomorphism.
Proof. Let δ≤i+1 C · denote the complex whose j-th term is C j if j ≤ i + 1
and 0 if j > i + 1:
                  δ≤i+1 C · : · · · → C i → C i+1 → 0 → · · · .
There is a natural surjection
                                C · → δ≤i+1 C ·
which for every ring homomorphism R → R′ (in particular the identity
R → R) induces an isomorphism
              H j (C · ⊗R R′ ) → H j (δ≤i+1 C · ⊗R R′ ), for j ≤ i.
                 54                   ABRAMOVICH, OLSSON, AND VISTOLI

                 Replacing C by δ≤i+1 C · we are then reduced to the case when C · is bounded
                 above, where the result is standard.                                      ♠

                   Appendix C. Another boundedness theorem for Hom-stacks
                                      By Martin Olsson
    AppendixB
                 C.1. Statement of Theorems.
         athm    Theorem C.2. Let B be a scheme, and let X and Y be Artin stacks of
                 finite presentation over B with finite diagonals. Assume that X is flat and
                 proper over B. Then:
                    (i) Let Hom(X , Y) denote the stack over B whose fiber over a B-scheme
                 T is the groupoid of T -morphisms of stacks
                                                 X ×B T → Y ×B T.
                 Then Hom(X , Y) is an algebraic stack locally of finite presentation over B,
                 with quasi-compact and separated diagonal.
                   (ii) Assume further that Y is a tame stack. If Y denotes the coarse moduli
                 space of Y, then the natural map
                                              Hom(X , Y) → Hom(X , Y )
                 is of finite type.
                 Remark C.3. If X is a tame stack, then the condition that X /B is flat
                 implies that the coarse moduli space X/B of X is also flat by [4, 3.3 (b)] and
                 its formation commutes with arbitrary base change by [4, 3.3]. It follows
                 that Hom(X, Y ) is an algebraic space locally of finite presentation over B,
            56                     ABRAMOVICH, OLSSON, AND VISTOLI

            and by the universal property of coarse moduli space there is a canonical
            isomorphism
                                      Hom(X , Y ) ≃ Hom(X, Y ).
                 In the context of C.2 one can also consider the substack
                                      Homrep (X , Y) ⊂ Hom(X , Y)
            classifying representable morphisms X → Y. As in [34, 1.6] this substack
            is an open substack, and therefore the following corollary follows from (C.2
            (ii)):
repfinite   Corollary C.4. With assumptions as in C.2, the natural map
                                     Homrep (X , Y) → Hom(X , Y )
            is of finite type.
               The rest of this appendix is devoted to the proof of C.2. By a standard
            limit argument, it suffices to consider the case when B is of finite type over
            an excellent Dedekind ring, which we assume henceforth.

    C.30    C.5. Algebraicity of Hom(X , Y). That Hom(X , Y) is an algebraic stack
            locally of finite presentation over B is shown in [6, 1.1] (see also the erratum
            [7]).
               For a morphism of stacks G → X over B, let
                                                Sec(G/X )
            denote the stack over B whose fiber over a B-scheme T is the groupoid of

            implies that if X /B is a proper flat algebraic stack with finite diagonal, and
            if G → X is a morphism of algebraic stacks with G a finitely presented Artin
            stack over B with finite diagonal, then the stack Sec(G/X ) is an algebraic
            stack locally of finite presentation over B, as it is equal to the fiber product
            of the diagram

    P:C6    C.6. The diagonal of Hom(X , Y ) is quasi-compact and separated. Under
            the assumptions of (C.2 (i)), we now show that the diagonal of Hom(X , Y)
            is quasi-compact and separated in the case when Y = Y is an algebraic
            space (the general case will be treated in C.13 below).
               To see that the diagonal of Hom(X , Y ) is separated, let
                                              f1 , f2 : X → Y
                                          TWISTED YET TAME                              57

            be two morphisms, and let I denote the fiber product of the diagram
                                                             B
                                                              f1 ×f2
                                                               
                                           ∆   // Hom(X , Y ) × Hom(X , Y ).
                            Hom(X , Y )
            The space I represents the functor on B-schemes which to any T /B asso-
            ciates the unital set if the base changes of the maps f1 and f2 to T are
            equal, and the empty set otherwise. In particular, the morphism I → B is
            a monomorphism, which implies that the diagonal
                                               I → I ×B I
            is an isomorphism. Therefore I is separated.
               To see that the diagonal of Hom(X , Y ) is quasi-compact, we may without
            loss of generality assume that B is reduced, and in this case it suffices by
            noetherian induction to exhibit a dense open subset of B over which I is
            quasi-compact. By shrinking on B we may therefore assume that the coarse
            moduli space X of X is flat over B, and that its formation commutes with
            arbitrary base change on B. In this case we have an isomorphism
                                     Hom(X , Y ) ≃ Hom(X, Y ),
            and the quasi-compactness of the diagonal follows from [39, 5.1].
               Next we use the results of appendix B to generalize three basic results
            about modifications in [39, §4], which will be necessary to proceed further
            in the proof of C.2.

            Passage to the maximal reduced substack.
            C.7. Let S be a noetherian scheme, and let G → X be a finite type morphism
            between Artin stacks of finite type over S with finite diagonals. Assume
            further that X is flat and proper over S.
finitelem   Proposition C.8. Let X0 ֒→ X be a closed immersion defined by a nilpotent
            ideal J ⊂ OX , and assume X0 is flat over S. Let G0 denote the base change
            G ×X X0 . Then the natural map
                                      Sec(G/X ) → Sec(G0 /X0 )
            is of finite type with quasi-compact diagonal.
            Proof. This is essentially the same as in [34, 5.11].
               By noetherian induction, it suffices to show that the morphism is of finite
            type with quasi-compact diagonal over a dense open subset of S. We may
            further assume that S is reduced (since if U and V are S-schemes locally
            of finite type and g : U → V is a morphism, then g is of finite type if and
            only if the base change of g to Sred is of finite type), and using the same
            argument given in [34, paragraph following proof of 5.11] that J 2 = 0.
             58                    ABRAMOVICH, OLSSON, AND VISTOLI

                It suffices to show that if T → Sec(G0 /X0 ) is a morphism corresponding
             to a section s : X0,T → G0,T , then the fiber product
                                      P := Sec(G/X ) ×Sec(G0 /X0 ) T
             is of finite type over T with quasi-compact diagonal. Furthermore, we may
             assume that T is an integral noetherian affine scheme. The stack P asso-
             ciates to any w : W → T the groupoid of liftings s̃ : XW → G over X of the
             composite
                                            X0,W → G0 → G,
             where the first map is the one induced by s.
               To prove that P is quasi–compact with quasi-compact diagonal, it suffices
             by Noetherian induction to exhibit a dense open set U ⊂ T such that PU is
             quasi–compact with quasi-compact diagonal.
               Let LG0 /X0 be the cotangent complex of G0 /X0 . By B.7, after replacing T
             by a dense open subscheme we may assume that the groups
                                    Exti (s∗ LG0 /X0 , J ), i = −1, 0, 1
             are projective modules on T of finite type, and that the formation of these
             modules commutes with arbitrary base change on T .
               By [38, 1.5] there is a canonical obstruction
                                         o ∈ Ext1 (s∗ LG0 /X0 , J )
             whose vanishing is necessary and sufficient for the existence of a lifting s̃
             as above, and the formation of this obstruction is functorial in T . After
             replacing T by the closed subscheme defined by the condition that o vanishes,
             we may assume that o = 0. In this case the set of isomorphism classes of
             liftings s̃ form a torsor under
                                           Ext0 (s∗ LG0 /X0 , J )
             and the group of infinitessimal automorphisms of s̃ is canonically isomorphic
             to
                                          Ext−1 (s∗ LG0 /X0 , J ).
             It follows that P is an Ext−1 (s∗ LG0 /X0 , J )–gerbe over

                                           Ext0 (s∗ LG0 /X0 , J ),
             and in particular is quasi–compact with quasi-compact diagonal.            ♠

             C.9. Let S be a noetherian scheme, and X /S a proper flat Artin stack with

finitecase   Proposition C.10. The stack Sec(G/X ) is an algebraic space separated and
             of finite type over S.

Proof. Let us first verify that the diagonal of Sec(G/X ) is separated and
quasi-compact. Equivalently, let
                                s1 , s2 : X → G
be two sections and let I denote the fiber product of the diagram

                               ∆

                  Sec(G/X )         // Sec(G/X ) × Sec(G/X ).

We need to show that I is quasi-compact and separated.
   That I is separated is immediate, for as in C.6 the fact that the map
G → X is representable implies that I is a subfunctor of B, and so the
diagonal of I/B is an isomorphism.
   To see the quasi-compactness of I, let Z ֒→ X be the closed substack
defined as the fiber product of the diagram (note that since G/X is separated
the diagonal of G/X is a closed immersion)
                                                G
                                                      ∆
                                   s1 ×s2        
                               X            // G ×X G.
Then I represents the functor which to any B-scheme T associates the unital
set if ZT = XT , and the empty set otherwise.
   Now to prove that I is quasi-compact, we can without loss of generality
replace S by Sred and hence may assume that S is reduced, and by noetherian
induction it suffices to show that the restriction of I to some dense open
subset of S is quasi-compact. We may therefore assume that S is integral,
and that the stack Z is flat over S. In this case I is isomorphic to an open
subset of S. Indeed let K denote the kernel of the surjection
                                   OX → OZ .
Since Z is flat over S, for any S-scheme T the sequence
                         0 → K → OX → OZ → 0
remains exact when pulled back to XT . It follows that if R ⊂ X denotes the
support of the coherent sheaf K, then I is represented by the complement
of the closed image (since X /S is proper) of R in S. This completes the
verification that the diagonal of Sec(G/X ) is quasi-compact and separated.
   To verify that Sec(G/X ) is of finite type over S, it suffices to show that
its pullback to Sred is of finite type. We may therefore assume that S is
reduced. Furthermore, we may by C.8 (applied with X0 = Xred ) assume
that X is also reduced. Furthermore, by noetherian induction it suffices to
exhibit a dense open subset of S over which Sec(G/X ) is of finite type.
   By Chow’s lemma for Artin stacks [37, 1.1], there exists a proper sur-
jection h : X ′ → X with X ′ a projective S-scheme. After shrinking on S
        60                    ABRAMOVICH, OLSSON, AND VISTOLI

        we may also assume that X ′ is flat over S (since S is reduced). Since X is
        reduced the map OX → h∗ OX ′ is injective. After shrinking on S, we may
        assume that the formation of h∗ OX ′ commutes with arbitrary base change
        S ′ → S, and that for any such base change the map OXS ′ → h∗ OX ′ ′ is also
                                                                                 S
        injective. Let G′ → X ′ denote the pullback G ×X X ′ .

            To verify that Sec(G/X ) is separated, note that since we already know

        valuative criterion for properness. This amounts to the following. Assume
        that S is the spectrum of a valuation ring and let η ∈ S be the generic point.
        Assume given two sections s1 , s2 : X → G whose restrictions to η are equal.
        Then we need to show that s1 = s2 . For this note that since G is finite over

          suffices to show that the composite maps

                                    A         // OX   // j∗ OXη

          are equal. Equivalently that the maps on the generic fiber

          are equal, which holds by assumption.                                       ♠

C.14. Reduction of (C.2 (ii)) to a special case.
C.15. Turning to the proof of (C.2 (ii)), note first that it suffices to show
that if f : X → Y is a morphism and G denotes the fiber product
                                G := X ×f,Y Y,
then the stack Sec(G/X ) is of finite type over B. This we do by a series of
reductions.
C.16. To prove that Sec(G/X ) is quasi-compact, it suffices by noetherian
induction to exhibit a dense open subset of B where this is so. Furthermore,
we may without loss of generality assume that B is integral. By Chow’s
lemma for Artin stacks [37, 1.1] there exists a proper surjection X ′ → X
with X ′ an algebraic space. After shrinking on B we may assume that X ′
is flat over B. Applying C.12 to the stack Sec(G/X ), we are then reduced
to proving that Sec(G ′ /X ′ ) is of finite type over B. This reduces to the case
when X is an algebraic space, which we assume for the rest of the proof
(and for consistency we write X instead of X ).
C.17. Furthermore, we can without loss of generality assume that B is in-
tegral. By noetherian induction, it suffices to exhibit a dominant morphism
B ′ → B such that the restriction of Sec(G/X) to B ′ is of finite type.
C.18. By the same argument used in [39, 6.4] we then reduce the proof of
(C.2 (ii)) to the case when X is integral and G → X has a section s : X → G.
Let Aut(s) denote the group scheme of automorphisms of s (a scheme over
X). Since X is reduced there exists a dense open subset U ⊂ X such that
the restriction of Aut(s) to U is flat over U . Let H ⊂ Aut(s) denote the
scheme–theoretic closure of Aut(s)|U . By [20, Premiére partie 5.2.2] there
exists a blow-up X ′ → X with center a proper closed subspace of X such that
                             TWISTED YET TAME                                63

the strict transform of H in Aut(s) is flat over X ′ . After further shrinking
on S we may assume that X ′ is flat over S. Since the map
                       Sec(G/X) → Sec(G ×X X ′ /X ′ )
is of finite type by C.12, we may therefore replace X by X ′ and hence can
assume that H is a finite flat subgroup scheme of Aut(s). Since all the
geometric fibers of H are linearly reductive being closed subgroup schemes
of linearly reductive groups (see [4, 2.7]), the X-group scheme H is in fact
                       e is the normalization of X the map
linearly reductive. If X
                        Sec(G/X) → Sec(G ×X X/   e X)
                                                    e
is also of finite type by C.12. This enables us to reduce to the following
situation: X is normal, s : X → G is a section, and H ⊂ Aut(s) is a finite
closed subgroup scheme which is flat and linearly reductive over X and over
a dense open subset of X the group scheme H is equal to Aut(s).
Lemma C.19. The morphism π : BH → G induced by s identifies BH with
the normalization of Gred .
Proof. Etale locally on X we can write G = [W/GLn ] for some n, where W
is an X–scheme. Indeed by [4, 3.2] we can étale locally on X write G =
[Z/G] with G a linearly reductive group scheme. Choosing any embedding
G ֒→ GLn we take W to be the quotient of Z × GLn by the diagonal action
of G.
   Let P → X be the pullback X ×s,G W . Then P is a GLn –torsor over X
with a GLn –equivariant morphism f : P → W . Since P is smooth over X
the space P is in particular normal, and since s is proper and quasi–finite
the morphism f is finite. After replacing X by an étale cover we may assume
given a section p ∈ P . Then Aut(s) is the closed subgroup scheme of GLn,X
given by the fiber product of the diagram
                           W × GLn
                                
                                
                               ρy

                                        ∆◦f ◦p
                               W × W ←−−−− X,
where ∆ : W → W × W is the diagonal and ρ is the map sending (v, g) to
(v, g(v)). In particular, we obtain an embedding H ⊂ GLn,X . Let P denote
the quotient P/H. The space P is normal. By the construction the map f
induces a morphism f¯ : P → W ∗ , where W ∗ denotes the normalization of
Wred . This map f¯ is finite, surjective, and birational and hence by Zariski’s
Main Theorem an isomorphism. On the other hand, we have P ≃ W ×G BH,
and hence if G ∗ denotes the normalization of Gred we find that the base
change of BH → G ∗ to W ×G G ∗ is an isomorphism. It follows that BH → G ∗
is an isomorphism.                                                           ♠
C.20. Let G ∗ denote the normalization of G, so that G ∗ is a gerbe over X.
As in [39, 3.14], after shrinking on B we may assume that for every field
       64                   ABRAMOVICH, OLSSON, AND VISTOLI

       valued point b ∈ B(k) the fiber Gb∗ → Gb is the normalization of Gb,red and
       that Xb is normal. It then follows that the map
                                 Sec(G ∗ /X) → Sec(G/X)
       is surjective on field valued points and hence surjective. We may therefore
       replace G by G ∗ and therefore may assume that G is a gerbe over X.
          Next we consider the case of a gerbe. If the generic point of B has
       characteristic 0, then after shrinking on B we can assume G is Deligne–
       Mumford in which case the result follows from [39, 1.1]. We may therefore
       assume that the generic point of B has characteristic p > 0, and hence
       after shrinking on B may assume that B is an Fp –scheme. In this case, for
       any B–scheme T and t ∈ G(T ), the automorphism group scheme Gt of t is
       canonically an extension
                                 1 → ∆t → Gt → Ht → 1,
       where ∆t is locally diagonalizable and Ht is étale over T . Indeed, the group
       scheme Gt is tame so we can take ∆t to be the subfunctor of Gt classifying
       elements of Gt killed by some power of p. This normal subgroup ∆t is
       functorial in the pair (T, t).
          Define H to be the stack (with respect to the fppf topology) associated to
       the prestack whose objects are the same as the objects of G but for which a
       morphism between two t, t′ ∈ G(T ) is defined to be the set
                  ∆t \Hom(t, t′ ) = ∆t \Hom(t, t′ )/∆t′ = Hom(t, t′ )/∆t′ .
       Then H is a Deligne–Mumford stack and there is a natural map G → H over
       X. By [39, 1.1] the stack Sec(H/X) is of finite type. On the other hand, for
       any section s : X → H, the fiber product
                                 Sec(G/X) ×Sec(H/X),s B
       is isomorphic to Sec(G ×H,s X/B). Now the stack G ×H,s X is a gerbe over
       X whose stabilizer groups are all diagonalizable. This further reduces the
       proof to the case when the Ht ’s in the above discussion are all trivial.
B.33   C.21. In this case, there exists a canonical locally diagonalizable group
       scheme ∆ on X such that G is bound by ∆. Indeed fppf locally on X there
       exists a section s : X → G giving rise to a group scheme ∆s . If s′ : X → G
       is a second section then locally s and s′ are isomorphic so we obtain an
       isomorphism ∆s ≃ ∆s′ . This isomorphism is independent of the choice of
       the isomorphism between s and s′ since ∆s and ∆s′ are abelian. It follows
       that the ∆s ’s descend to a group scheme ∆ on X.
          Since the Cartier dual of ∆ is a locally constant sheaf of finite abelian
       groups on Xet , there exists a finite étale covering X ′ → X such that the
       pullback of ∆ to X ′ is a diagonalizable group scheme. Since
                              Sec(G/X) → Sec(G ×X X ′ /X ′ )
       is of finite type by C.12, this reduces the proof to the case when G is a gerbe
       over X bound by a diagonalizable group scheme ∆. In other words, when G
                                        TWISTED YET TAME                                 65

           corresponds to a cohomology class in H 2 (X, ∆). Write ∆ = µn1 × · · · × µnr
           so that                             Y
                                 H 2 (X, ∆) =     H 2 (X, µni ).
                                                   i
           Using the resulting decomposition of the cohomology class of G, we see that
           G is isomorphic to a product G1 ×X · · · ×X Gr , where Gi is a µni –gerbe over
           X. Then                              Y
                                   Sec(G/X) ≃       Sec(Gi /X).
                                                   i
           This therefore finally reduces the proof to the case of a µn –gerbe over X
           which is the case treated in the following subsection.
Gtwisted
           C.22. G–twisted line bundles.
  case1    C.23. Fix an integer n. Assume that X = X and that G is a µn –gerbe
           over X. Assume furthermore that if f : X → B denotes the structural
           morphism then the map OB → f∗ OX is an isomorphism, and the same
           remains true after arbitrary base change B ′ → B. This implies that for any
           scheme T and object s ∈ G(T ) we have an isomorphism µn ≃ Aut(s) and
           these isomorphisms are functorial in the pair (T, s). If L is a line bundle
           on G then for any such pair (T, s) we obtain a line bundle s∗ L on T which
           also comes equipped with an action of µn = Aut(s). The line bundle L is
           called a G–twisted invertible sheaf on X if this action of µn coincides with
           the standard action induced by the embedding µn ֒→ Gm .
              Note that if χ denotes the standard character µn ֒→ Gm then for any line
           bundle L on G the action of µn = Aut(s) on s∗ L is given by χi for some
           integer i (locally constant on T ). It follows that to check that a line bundle
           L is G–twisted it suffices to verify that the two actions coincide for pairs
           (T, s) with T the spectrum of an algebraically closed field.
              If L is a G–twisted sheaf on X, then L⊗n descends canonically to an
           invertible sheaf on X since the stabilizer actions of µn are trivial. We usually
           write just L⊗n for the sheaf on X obtained from L⊗n .
   B.18    Proposition C.24. There is a natural equivalence between Sec(G/X) and
           the stack which to any B–scheme T associates the groupoid of pairs (L, ι),
           where L is a G–twisted sheaf on X and ι : L⊗n ≃ OX is an isomorphism of
           invertible sheaves on X.
           Proof. If s : X → G is a section, then there is a canonical action of µn =
           Aut(s) on F := s∗ OX and hence F decomposes canonically as ⊕χ∈Z/(n) Fχ .
           Lemma C.25. Each Fχ is locally free of rank 1 on G and for any two
           χ, ǫ ∈ Z/(n) the natural map Fχ ⊗ Fǫ → Fχ+ǫ is an isomorphism. If
           χ1 : µn → Gm denotes the standard inclusion, then Fχ1 is a G–twisted sheaf
           on X.
           Proof. The choice of the section s identifies G with BAut(s) ≃ Bµn × X.
           The fiber product X ×s,Bµn,s X is equal to X × Bµn from which we see that
           66                   ABRAMOVICH, OLSSON, AND VISTOLI

           s∗ F is equal to OX ⊗Z Z[X]/(X n − 1) with the natural action of µn . From
           this the lemma follows.                                                  ♠
             In particular, by sending a section s : X → G to Fχ1 with the isomorphism
           Fχ⊗n
              1
                ≃ OG we obtain a functor
sectwist   (C.25.1)           Sec(G/X) → (stack of pairs (L, ι) as in C.24).
           Conversely, given a G–twisted sheaf L with an isomorphism ι : L⊗n ≃ OX

                              ⊗i
           the natural maps L ⊗ L → L⊗j     ⊗i+j and the map ι. We can then consider
                                          SpecG (A) → G.
           If G = Bµn ×X and X → G is the map defined by the trivial torsor, then the
           restriction of (L, ι) to X is an invertible sheaf L on X with an isomorphism
                                                                                 n−1 ⊗i
           L⊗n ≃ OX and the restriction of A to X is just the cyclic algebra ⊕i=0   L
                               ⊗i                                 i
           with µn acting L through the character u 7→ u . It follows that the
           projection SpecG (A) → X is an isomorphism and hence defines a point of
           Sec(G/X). We leave to the reader that this defines an inverse to C.25.1. ♠
             Let PicGX/B denote the stack over B which to any B–scheme T associates
           the groupoid of GT –twisted invertible sheaves on XT (where GT denotes
           G ×B T etc.).
           Proposition C.26. (i) The stack PicGX/B is an algebraic stack locally of
           finite presentation over B.
              (ii) The sheaf (with respect to the fppf topology) associated to the presheaf
                              T 7→ {isomorphism classes in PicGX/B }
           is representable by a separated algebraic space locally of finite presentation
           over B.
           Proof. This follows for example by the same argument used in [8, Appendix].
                                                                                    ♠
           C.27. There is a natural morphism
  Picmap   (C.27.1)               PicGX/B → PicX/B , L 7→ L⊗n .

           Denote by PicGX/B [n] the inverse image of the identity e = [OX ] ∈ PicX/B .
           Another description of this space is as follows. The map C.27.1 lifts naturally
           to a morphism
                               π ∗ : PicGX/B → PicX/B , L 7→ L⊗n .
           Let e : B → PicX/B be the morphism corresponding to OX , and set
                                 PicGX/B [n] := PicGX/B ×PicX/B ,e B.

           The stack PicGX/B [n] classifies pairs (L, ι), where L is a G–twisted sheaf
           on X and ι : L⊗n ≃ OX is an isomorphism. The space PicGX/B [n] is the
                                          TWISTED YET TAME                                   67

           coarse moduli space of PicGX/B [n] via the map sending (L, ι) to the class of
           L. In fact, PicGX/B [n] is a µn –gerbe over PicGX/S [n]. Indeed any point P of
           PicGX/B [n](B) can fppf–locally on B be represented by a G–twisted sheaf L
           with L⊗n ≃ OX . Conversely for any two pairs (L, ι) and (L′ , ι′ ) defining
           the same point of PicGX/B [n], the two G–twisted sheaves L and L′ become
           isomorphic after making an fppf base change on B. Then ι and ι′ differ by a
           section of f∗ OG∗ ≃ Gm . After making another fppf base change on B so that
           this unit becomes an n–th power, the two pairs (L, ι) and (L′ , ι′ ) become
           isomorphic. Moreover, this isomorphism is unique up to multiplication by
           an element of µn (B).
           Proposition C.28. The algebraic space PicGX/B [n] is of finite type over B.
           Proof. To prove this statement it suffices by a standard limit argument to
           consider the case when B is a noetherian scheme. In this case by noetherian
           induction it suffices to find a dominant morphism B ′ → B such that the
           restriction of PicGX/B to B ′ is of finite type. We may therefore also assume
           that B is a noetherian affine integral scheme. By Chow’s lemma there exists
           a proper surjection P → G with P an algebraic space. After shrinking on B
           we may assume that P is also flat over B. Then G ×X P is trivial and by
           C.12 the pullback map
                    Sec(G/X) ≃ PicGX/B [n] → PicGG×X P/P [n] ≃ Sec(G ×X P/P )
           is of finite type. Consequently the map
                                        PicGX/B [n] → PicGP/B [n]
           is also of finite type. It therefore suffices to show PicGP/B [n] is of finite type.
              Now in the case when G = Bµn × X there exists a globally defined G-
           twisted sheaf L with L⊗n trivial. Choose one such sheaf L. If p : G → X
           denotes the projection, then for any invertible sheaf M on X with M⊗n ≃
           OX , the sheaf L ⊗ p∗ M is also a G–twisted sheaf. Conversely, if N is
           a G–twisted sheaf with N ⊗n trivial, then L ⊗ N −1 descends uniquely to
           an n–torsion sheaf on X. Using this one sees that PicGX/B [n] is a trivial
           torsor under PicX/B [n]. The proposition therefore follows from [25, 6.27
           and 6.28].                                                                        ♠
proofend   C.29. Since Sec(G/X) ≃ PicGX/B [n] is a µn –gerbe over PicGX/B [n] this com-
           pletes the proof of (C.2 (ii)) in the special case of C.23 and hence also the
           proof in general.                                                          ♠
